title: Violent relaxation redux
summary: Collisionless self-gravitating systems, such as merging galaxies, have long seemed an exception to the statistical-mechanical principle that chaotic many-body systems relax to maximum-entropy states: Lynden-Bell's statistical mechanics of their "violent relaxation," constrained by exact conservation of phase-space volume -- equivalently, of infinitely many collisionless "Casimir" invariants -- has appeared not to be a good description. We propose that violent relaxation does give rise to Lynden-Bell's maximum-entropy equilibria, but that both are underpinned by gravitational turbulence, in which large-scale gravitational fluctuations drive chaotic phase-space mixing of the particles' distribution function. We derive the universal small-scale (sub-Jeans) spectra of this turbulence and show that it leads to phase-space-volume conservation being broken on a timescale only logarithmically longer, in the particle number N, than the dynamical (violent-relaxation) time. This timescale separation lets the system relax "adiabatically" through a sequence of Lynden-Bell equilibria, each corresponding to instantaneous values of the Casimirs. At long times, it approaches an equilibrium close to its "ground state": a distribution whose Casimirs have adjusted so that the system's energy is now its minimum possible energy. Thus, the system's universal tendency is toward a minimum-energy, maximum-entropy state. We corroborate this picture with 1D N-body simulations and hypothesize that it can explain the universal equilibria of galaxies and dark-matter halos.

The authors derive turbulence spectra and timescale arguments and corroborate the picture with 1D N-body simulations.
AI.motivation: Collisionless self-gravitating systems such as merging galaxies have appeared inconsistent with relaxation to maximum-entropy states because Lynden-Bell's statistical mechanics of violent relaxation requires exact conservation of phase-space volume, or equivalently infinitely many collisionless Casimir invariants, and has seemed to describe these systems poorly. The paper aims to reconcile violent relaxation with Lynden-Bell maximum-entropy equilibria.

They corroborate the scenario with 1D N-body simulations. Specific simulation parameters and quantitative details are not provided in the abstract.

title: Domain-Adapted Deep Optical Flow for Multiphase Velocimetry in Unsteady Cloud Cavitation
comment: 39 pages, 17 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to Experiments in Fluids
summary: Time-resolved velocimetry inside cloud cavitation remains a fundamental measurement problem. We present a domain-adapted deep optical flow framework for two-phase velocimetry, built on a Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms (RAFT) architecture fine-tuned on synthetic image pairs rendered from multiphase OpenFOAM simulations (RAFT-CloudCav). It is evaluated against a pre-trained generalist RAFT model, Farnebäck and OpenPIV on 130,000 frames/s recordings of a Venturi test section at 30 and 48 L/min. As no experimental ground truth exists, validation uses three quantities that require none, namely the integrated flow rate against a turbine meter, the liquid-phase velocity divergence, which mass conservation requires to vanish, and the station-to-station spread of the flow rate. RAFT-CloudCav recovers 47.75 L/min against a metered 48.0 $\pm$ 0.5 L/min, the closest of the four methods, and its flow rate varies by 2.0% across four streamwise stations, versus 6-7% for the classical methods. It returns a coherent near-wall reverse flow of -0.71 m/s, the time-averaged signature of the upstream-propagating re-entrant jet, where OpenPIV returns none. In the non-cavitating control, at 51 $μ$m/pixel only three grid points fall inside a 0.68 mm boundary layer and the peak wall-normal gradient is under-predicted more than thirtyfold, while 13 and 19 $μ$m/pixel agree with each other. The mean field is recovered without tracer particles at roughly three times the per-frame uncertainty. Uncertainties are estimated a posteriori from the image residual and propagated conservatively.

title: Layer-Peeling Inversion of Temporal Refractive Index Profiles from Noisy Data
summary: We introduce a direct method for reconstructing the temporal evolution of a medium from electromagnetic field measurements. A sequence of temporal refractive-index changes splits an incident wave into forward- and backward-propagating components, producing a \emph{spatial} response of finite extent. We show that this finite support, together with causality, enables sequential reconstruction of the temporal interfaces through a time-domain extension of layer peeling. For continuously varying media, we introduce a time-adjusted Goupillaud medium and, through space-time duality, establish the corresponding momentum-conservation and admissibility conditions. The method remains robust under incomplete and noisy measurements, providing a general framework for the metrology, characterization, and design of time-varying electromagnetic systems.

Combined with causality, this enables sequential reconstruction of temporal interfaces via a time-domain extension of layer peeling. For continuously varying media, the authors introduce a time-adjusted Goupillaud medium and use space-time duality to establish momentum-conservation and admissibility conditions.

title: Existence of Distinct Strong and Weak Shear Regimes of Self-Generated Turbulent Magnetic Reconnection
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, accepted for the Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: Magnetic reconnection can become fast in three-dimensional turbulent layers. However, the parameters and mechanisms that control the fast state are not yet fully clear. Existing guide-field simulations of self-generated turbulent reconnection show locally coherent flux-rope structures embedded in a stochastic layer, motivating a flux-rope-mediated picture, with reconnection rates of order $V_{\rm rec}/V_A \sim 0.01$ in MHD. Here, we test whether and how magnetic shear changes the reconnection regime, using 3D resistive-MHD simulations at $S_L=10^5$. We vary the guide field while keeping the initial reconnecting field strength and rate normalization fixed, comparing a guide-field, weaker-shear configuration with the anti-parallel, strong-shear limit. We find that the strong-shear regime is qualitatively distinct from the flux-rope-mediated guide-field regime. Rather than retaining a narrow layer and locally coherent flux-rope structures, the current layer develops short-wavelength corrugations that broaden it substantially, and the reconnection layer electric field is sustained by fluctuation EMF. The reconnection rate increases to $V_{\rm rec}/V_A \sim 0.03$, about three times the guide-field value. These results indicate that magnetic shear can select the mechanism controlling fast 3D turbulent reconnection, shifting the system from a guide-field regime consistent with flux-rope mediation toward a very fast turbulence-broadened regime. This transition provides a novel explanation for the sudden switch-on of fast reconnection in eruptive solar flares.

AI.method: The authors perform 3D resistive-MHD simulations at S_L=10^5, varying the guide field while holding the initial reconnecting field strength and rate normalization fixed. They compare a guide-field, weaker-shear configuration with the anti-parallel, strong-shear limit.

Its current layer develops short-wavelength corrugations and broadens substantially, its reconnection-layer electric field is sustained by the fluctuation EMF, and its reconnection rate reaches V_rec/V_A ~ 0.03, about three times the guide-field value of ~0.01.

title: Sub-filter-scale stress and heat flux in hypersonic Couette flow and a flat-plate boundary layer
comment: Submitted to the Journal of Fluid Mechanics; currently under review
summary: A comparative study of sub-filter-scale (SFS) quantities in hypersonic Couette flow and flat-plate boundary layer turbulence under strongly cooled-wall conditions is carried out using filtered direct numerical simulation (DNS) data to characterize the differences in SFS dynamics between internal and external wall-bounded turbulence. The two flows exhibit similar near-wall behaviour in the mean velocity profiles and SFS stress components; however, marked differences emerge in the outer layer and thermal structure. The two configurations also exhibit different thermal fields, leading to different temperature-velocity relations. The SFS behaviour shows strong sensitivity to the filtering operation: the top-hat filter yields larger SFS magnitudes, whereas the sharp spectral filter preserves a distinct spectral separation near the cutoff, leading to characteristic SFS features. Decomposition of the SFS terms shows that the residual component provides the dominant contribution to the mean SFS shear stress and heat flux. Differences between the two flows are primarily associated with the interaction terms between the resolved and residual components, which contribute with opposite signs in the two configurations, consistent with their different thermal structures. The different thermal structures also lead to distinct SFS heat-flux behaviour, including a sign change in the flat-plate boundary layer. Instantaneous SFS fields further reveal that local extrema arise from the combined contributions of multiple decomposed terms. Although these terms exhibit large local fluctuations, their net contributions to the averaged SFS quantities are relatively small. The trace of the SFS stress exhibits local negative values, reflecting local energy redistribution across the filter scale rather than a loss of physical energy.

AI.tldr: Filtered DNS data are used to compare sub-filter-scale stress and heat-flux dynamics in hypersonic Couette flow and a flat-plate boundary layer with strongly cooled walls, revealing near-wall similarities but outer-layer and thermal-structure differences, strong filter sensitivity, and dominant residual-component contributions.
AI.motivation: The study aims to characterize differences in sub-filter-scale dynamics between internal and external wall-bounded turbulence under hypersonic, strongly cooled-wall conditions.
AI.method: The authors perform a comparative analysis using filtered direct numerical simulation data for hypersonic Couette flow and a flat-plate boundary layer. They examine mean velocity and thermal fields, SFS stress and heat-flux components, top-hat versus sharp spectral filtering, decomposition of SFS terms into resolved, residual, and interaction contributions, and instantaneous SFS fields.
AI.result: The two flows show similar near-wall mean velocity profiles and SFS stress components, but differ markedly in the outer layer and thermal structure, producing different temperature-velocity relations. The top-hat filter yields larger SFS magnitudes, while the sharp spectral filter preserves spectral separation near the cutoff. The residual component dominates the mean SFS shear stress and heat flux; interaction terms between resolved and residual components have opposite signs in the two configurations and are linked to their different thermal structures. The flat-plate boundary layer exhibits a sign change in SFS heat flux. Instantaneous fields show that local extrema arise from multiple decomposed terms, whose net averaged contributions are relatively small. Negative local values of the SFS stress trace reflect local energy redistribution across the filter scale rather than physical energy loss.
AI.conclusion: The study clarifies how internal and external wall-bounded hypersonic turbulence differ in SFS dynamics, emphasizing the roles of thermal structure, filter choice, and residual-interaction decomposition; it does not report a new SFS model.

title: A hair-thin implant opens the entire depth of the mouse brain to revisiting the same structures at subcellular resolution
comment: These authors contributed equally: Miroslav Stibůrek, Tomáš Pikálek, Petra Ondráčková Corresponding authors: Hana Uhlířová (huhlirova@isibrno.cz) and Tomáš Čižmár (cizmart@isibrno.cz)
summary: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the depth of the mouse brain. Here we introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 μm, about the thickness of a human hair, that extends this capability to longitudinal imaging, enabling repeated access to the same fine structures over extended periods. The system supports weeks-long tracking of individual dendritic spines, allowing quantitative comparison of their dynamics and survival across dendritic compartments. We further demonstrate longitudinal intracellular calcium imaging during spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the same cells across days, as well as repeated measurements of blood flow in the same vessels across multiple brain regions. This chronic endomicroscopic platform provides stable, minimally invasive optical access for longitudinal subcellular-resolution imaging of brain structure, activity and blood flow across depth.

AI.motivation: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the mouse brain, but the work aims to extend this capability to longitudinal imaging so that the same fine structures can be revisited repeatedly over extended periods.
AI.method: The authors introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 μm, approximately the thickness of a human hair, based on an ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscope. title: An Analytical Model for Laser-Activated Two-Phase Choking and Microfluidic Suction on Surface Boundary Layers
comment: Submitted for publication. The source code used to produce Figure 2 is hosted openly at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23134296
summary: We present a predictive fluid mechanics model to calculate pressure drops (0.25 atm) and fluid velocities (2.50 m/s) governed by localized phase change and choking phenomena in a capillary-constrained, coaxial microfluidic actuator. Driven by near-infrared thermal absorption, the analytical framework describes how energy deposition drives vapor cavity growth and subsequent cavitation bubble collapse, inducing a transient suction force across a curved, two-radii Young-Laplace capillary boundary. Velocity drops are derived from closed-form analytical equations that explicitly couple vapor volume dynamics with non-linear flow area restriction and fluid drag. The model predicts a maximum boundary layer wall shear stress of 30.06 Pa at the target interface. Crucially, this shear magnitude matches the physical threshold required to mechanically strip surface contaminant boundary layers while remaining below the damage threshold of underlying target substrates. Finally, we formulate a closed-form expression for the maximum allowable liquid inlet temperature required to prevent thermal saturation and sustain stable, continuous microfluidic suction cycles. These equations establish direct engineering design rules for optimizing phase-change microfluidic actuators and next-generation coaxial fluidic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an analytical fluid-mechanics model for a near-infrared laser-activated, capillary-constrained coaxial microfluidic actuator, predicting phase-change-driven choking, suction, pressure drops, velocities, boundary-layer shear, and a thermal-saturation limit for stable operation.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to provide a predictive framework and direct engineering design rules for optimizing laser-activated phase-change microfluidic actuators and next-generation coaxial fluidic systems, including operation that can strip contaminant boundary layers without damaging underlying substrates.
AI.method: A closed-form analytical model couples vapor cavity growth and cavitation bubble collapse with non-linear flow-area restriction, fluid drag, and a curved two-radii Young-Laplace capillary boundary under near-infrared thermal absorption. It derives velocity drops, pressure drops, boundary-layer wall shear stress, and a closed-form maximum allowable liquid inlet temperature to prevent thermal saturation.

This shear is reported to match the threshold for mechanically stripping surface contaminant boundary layers while remaining below the damage threshold of underlying substrates. A closed-form maximum allowable liquid inlet temperature is formulated, but its numerical value is not provided in the abstract.

title: Breathers across the Focusing-to-Defocusing Transition: From Diffraction-Like Dynamics to Talbot Carpets
summary: We experimentally investigate fundamental unstable breather wave groups propagating across the transition from focusing to defocusing regimes. In hydrodynamics, this transition is realized through a rapid reduction in water depth over a short spatial interval. We demonstrate that the time-periodic Akhmediev breather develops a Talbot-like recurrence pattern in the defocusing regime, although only its initial stages are experimentally accessible. In contrast, the Peregrine breather exhibits qualitatively different behavior, characterized by oscillatory envelope dynamics. These oscillations can be understood as a purely linear phenomenon arising within the nonlinear Schrödinger framework when dispersion dominates over nonlinearity, as further confirmed by numerical simulations over extended propagation distances. The experimental observations agree closely with finite-depth nonlinear Schrödinger predictions across regimes with substantially different relative strengths of dispersion and nonlinearity. Our findings reveal a temporal analogue of diffraction and provide a foundation for exploring focusing-to-defocusing transitions in other nonlinear dispersive media.

AI.tldr: Experiments in a hydrodynamic platform with a rapid water-depth reduction show how unstable breather wave groups behave across the focusing-to-defocusing transition: Akhmediev breathers develop Talbot-like recurrence in the defocusing regime, while Peregrine breathers show oscillatory envelope dynamics consistent with dispersion-dominated linear behavior within the nonlinear Schrödinger framework.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to experimentally investigate fundamental unstable breather wave groups propagating across the transition from focusing to defocusing regimes and to establish a temporal analogue of diffraction, providing a basis for studying such transitions in other nonlinear dispersive media.
AI.method: The focusing-to-defocusing transition is realized in hydrodynamics by rapidly reducing water depth over a short spatial interval. Experimental observations are compared with finite-depth nonlinear Schrödinger predictions across regimes with substantially different relative strengths of dispersion and nonlinearity, and numerical simulations are used over extended propagation distances.
AI.result: The time-periodic Akhmediev breather develops a Talbot-like recurrence pattern in the defocusing regime, although only its initial stages are experimentally accessible. The Peregrine breather instead exhibits qualitatively different oscillatory envelope dynamics, interpretable as a purely linear phenomenon arising within the nonlinear Schrödinger framework when dispersion dominates over nonlinearity. Experimental observations agree closely with finite-depth nonlinear Schrödinger predictions.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a temporal analogue of diffraction and provide a foundation for exploring focusing-to-defocusing transitions in other nonlinear dispersive media.

title: Redetermination of the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BaMgF4
summary: BaMgF4 (BMF) has the potential to serve as a platform material for vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) nonlinear optics owing to its ferroelectricity and high UV transparency down to 130 nm. However, the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients reported for BMF span approximately one order of magnitude, hindering a reliable assessment of its potential for nonlinear optical applications. Here, we redetermined these coefficients by combining Maker fringe, wedge, and single-pass second-harmonic-generation measurements at a fundamental wavelength of 1064 nm. Our results establish that all the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BMF lie in the range of 0.01-0.04 pm/V. We determined d31 to be 0.035 pm/V, which is among the largest coefficients of BMF, while it has been underestimated relative to the other coefficients in previous studies. Although d31 is not the largest coefficient, the use of its long corresponding coherence length is beneficial for quasi-phase matching, particularly for VUV generation, where the fabrication of lower-order quasi-phase-matching structures is crucial.

AI.method: The authors combined Maker fringe, wedge, and single-pass second-harmonic-generation measurements at a fundamental wavelength of 1064 nm to redetermine the second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BaMgF4.
AI.result: All second-order nonlinear optical coefficients of BaMgF4 were found to lie in the range 0.01–0.04 pm/V. The d31 coefficient was determined to be 0.035 pm/V, among the largest coefficients of BaMgF4, although it had been underestimated relative to other coefficients in previous studies.
AI.conclusion: The redetermined coefficients provide a more reliable basis for assessing BaMgF4 for nonlinear optics. Although d31 is not the largest coefficient, its long coherence length is beneficial for quasi-phase matching, particularly for vacuum-ultraviolet generation where lower-order quasi-phase-matching structures are important.

title: Evaporation-induced colloidal diffusiophoresis in electrolyte solutions
summary: Non-volatile solutes accumulate near a receding drying front, generating concentration gradients that can drive directional colloidal transport by diffusiophoresis. This dynamic spatial arrangement of colloidal particles could affect the microstructure and macroscopic properties of the dried film. Here, we combine experiments and theory to investigate polystyrene particles suspended in electrolyte solutions drying within a capillary tube. By varying the electrolyte composition and ambient relative humidity, we show that evaporation-induced ion gradients drive particles toward the liquid-gas interface and enhance interfacial accumulation, whereas slower drying at higher humidity weakens the gradient and particle migration. We use the heat balance integral method to predict the transient solute field for a receding interface and couple it to particle transport to capture the observed particle trajectories and accumulation trends. These results identify background electrolytes and drying rate as coupled controls on particle distribution and provide a predictive framework to optimize formulation and processing parameters for manufacturing slurry-based materials, such as battery electrodes and turbine coatings.

AI.tldr: Experiments and theory show that evaporation-induced ion gradients in drying electrolyte solutions drive colloidal diffusiophoresis, enhancing particle accumulation at the liquid–gas interface; the effect weakens at higher humidity and slower drying.
AI.motivation: Non-volatile solutes accumulating near a receding drying front create concentration gradients that can drive directional colloidal transport, potentially altering the microstructure and macroscopic properties of dried films. The paper aims to understand and predict this coupled transport.
AI.method: The authors combine experiments and theory using polystyrene particles suspended in electrolyte solutions drying within a capillary tube. They vary electrolyte composition and ambient relative humidity, and use the heat balance integral method to predict the transient solute field for a receding interface, coupling it to particle transport.
AI.result: Evaporation-induced ion gradients drive particles toward the liquid–gas interface and enhance interfacial accumulation, whereas slower drying at higher humidity weakens the gradient and particle migration. The coupled model captures the observed particle trajectories and accumulation trends.
AI.conclusion: Background electrolytes and drying rate are coupled controls on particle distribution. The study provides a predictive framework for optimizing formulation and processing parameters in slurry-based materials such as battery electrodes and turbine coatings.

title: When is an Optical Design Problem a Mass Transfer Problem?
summary: This paper investigates whether optical design problems can be represented as Monge--Kantorovich mass transfer problems with some cost function. An optical problem is specified by a function defining a particular family of supporting surfaces for the optical element. We introduce the notion of geometric equivalence between optical and transport problems, which is directly related to the possibility of formulating an optical design problem as a mass transfer problem. A necessary condition for such equivalence is derived in the semi-discrete setting. It allows a transport representation to be ruled out without choosing a cost function in advance. The condition is applied to the near-field refractor problem and to the design of two refracting surfaces transforming a spherical beam into a spherical or collimated beam. For these problems, the necessary condition is shown to fail in physically admissible configurations. We also study an optical element with a single working surface and an arbitrary regular incident wavefront. In the far field, geometric equivalence to a mass transfer problem requires a planar or spherical wavefront, whereas in the near field with a planar target, the necessary condition fails for an arbitrary smooth wavefront.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when an optical design problem can be formulated as a Monge–Kantorovich mass transfer problem. It introduces geometric equivalence, derives a necessary condition in the semi-discrete setting, and applies it to refractor and two-surface beam-shaping problems. The condition rules out transport representations for several physically admissible configurations; far-field equivalence requires planar or spherical incident wavefronts.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to determine whether optical design problems admit a representation as Monge–Kantorovich mass transfer problems with some cost function, and to obtain a criterion that can rule out such a transport representation without first choosing a cost function.
AI.method: The authors define geometric equivalence between an optical design problem, specified by a family of supporting surfaces, and a mass transfer problem. They derive a necessary condition for this equivalence in the semi-discrete setting and apply it to the near-field refractor problem, to the design of two refracting surfaces transforming a spherical beam into a spherical or collimated beam, and to an optical element with one working surface and an arbitrary regular incident wavefront in the near and far fields.
AI.result: For the near-field refractor problem and the two-refracting-surface beam-shaping problems, the necessary condition fails in physically admissible configurations, ruling out geometric equivalence to mass transfer. For a single working surface with arbitrary regular incident wavefront, far-field equivalence requires a planar or spherical wavefront, while in the near field with a planar target the necessary condition fails for an arbitrary smooth wavefront.
AI.conclusion: Geometric equivalence between optical design and Monge–Kantorovich mass transfer is not universal: the derived necessary condition excludes transport formulations for several optical problems and imposes restrictive wavefront requirements in the far field. The abstract does not provide a general sufficient condition or numerical examples.

title: An acousto-optic colorimeter for color psychophysics
summary: A complete model of human color perception requires the ability to present any color as a stimulus.Most existing measurements were collected with physical color samples, and current laboratory generators, such as displays and multi-primary LED systems, work with a small number of fixed primaries. Published color-difference data therefore cover about 40\% of the CIE~$xy$ chromaticity diagram, while commercial wide-gamut displays already reach two thirds of it and need difference metrics there. We describe an acousto-optic colorimeter that lets the experimenter choose the primaries. The device selects up to four narrow bands from a supercontinuum (white-light) laser, each with electronically set wavelength and intensity, and covers 95\% of the CIE~$xy$ chromaticity diagram. Threshold-scale color differences, presented in alternation as in a discrimination experiment, are reproduced with a mean error of 0.08--0.12 CIEDE2000 units ($ΔE_{00}$) at five CIE-recommended color centers. Because one color can be built from many combinations of narrow bands, the bands are chosen for the task: the finest adjustment for color matching, the least disagreement between observers for color-difference measurement. In simulations with 151~individual observers from a published dataset, with these bands observers see colors 0.6--1.9~$ΔE_{00}$ from the intended one on average, against 1.2--2.5~$ΔE_{00}$ on a calibrated wide-gamut LCD, lower at every center. The approach applies to any narrowband source and lets experimenters use saturated colors while limiting the effect of individual differences in color vision.

AI.tldr: The paper describes an acousto-optic colorimeter that selects up to four electronically tunable narrow bands from a supercontinuum white-light laser to generate color stimuli across 95% of the CIE xy chromaticity diagram, enabling threshold-scale color-difference measurements with low error and reduced observer variability.
AI.motivation: Existing color-difference data cover only about 40% of the CIE xy chromaticity diagram because most measurements use physical samples or fixed-primary displays and LED systems, whereas commercial wide-gamut displays already reach about two thirds of the diagram and require difference metrics in that region. A complete model of human color perception also requires the ability to present any color as a stimulus.
AI.method: The acousto-optic colorimeter selects up to four narrow bands from a supercontinuum white-light laser, with each band's wavelength and intensity set electronically. The bands can be chosen for the task: finest adjustment for color matching or least disagreement between observers for color-difference measurement. Threshold-scale color differences were presented in alternation as in a discrimination experiment at five CIE-recommended color centers, and simulations used 151 individual observers from a published dataset to compare performance with a calibrated wide-gamut LCD.
AI.result: The device covers 95% of the CIE xy chromaticity diagram and reproduces threshold-scale color differences with a mean error of 0.08–0.12 CIEDE2000 units at five CIE-recommended color centers. In simulations with 151 observers, the chosen narrow bands produced average errors of 0.6–1.9 ΔE00 from the intended color, versus 1.2–2.5 ΔE00 on a calibrated wide-gamut LCD, with lower error at every center.
AI.conclusion: The approach applies to any narrowband source and lets experimenters use saturated colors while limiting the effect of individual differences in color vision. No laser–plasma interaction or intense-laser strong-field application is described.

title: Raytracing and quantifying the inferior mirage
summary: Using custom raytracing code, we explore several features of the inferior mirage that are not widely discussed, such as the blurring in the mirage image, and what happens to the light in the direct image region that is replaced by the mirage image. The raytracing model also clarifies how to quantify the mirage, and we provide expressions to calculate the angular extent of the mirage under given thermal conditions and measurement geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper uses custom raytracing code to examine underdiscussed features of the inferior mirage, including image blurring and the light in the direct-image region replaced by the mirage, and derives expressions for its angular extent from thermal conditions and measurement geometry.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to explore inferior-mirage features that are not widely discussed and to clarify how the mirage can be quantified.
AI.method: A custom raytracing model is used to analyze the mirage image, blurring, the direct image region, and the behavior of light; expressions are provided for calculating the angular extent of the mirage under given thermal conditions and measurement geometry.
AI.result: The raytracing model clarifies inferior-mirage blurring and what happens to light in the direct image region replaced by the mirage, and it yields expressions for the mirage’s angular extent. No quantitative experimental validation or specific numerical results are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Raytracing provides a useful basis for understanding and quantifying the inferior mirage, including its angular extent under specified thermal and geometric conditions.

title: Optical microscopy for pathological imaging: past, present, and future
summary: Histopathology, the microscopic examination of stained tissue sections, remains the gold standard for pathology imaging, but its bright-field imaging is largely morphological. Advanced optical microscopy techniques move beyond this by exploiting diverse light-matter interactions, and are increasingly applied to pathological imaging. By capturing signals such as refractive index, polarisation, harmonic generation, Brillouin shift, and molecular vibrations, these microscopy techniques can provide quantitative or semi-quantitative information on tissue structure, mechanics, and chemical or molecular composition. In this review, we summarise the physical principles, key quantitative parameters, and representative pathological applications of seven modalities--optical diffraction tomography, polarisation microscopy, second-harmonic generation microscopy, third-harmonic generation microscopy, Brillouin microscopy, Raman microscopy, and fluorescence microscopy. We also discuss progress in artificial intelligence that supports reconstruction, analysis, and interpretation across these modalities, together with emerging trends in multimodal integration. Overall, this review shows how different optical contrasts can complement routine histopathology, while outlining the challenges and opportunities that will shape their clinical translation.

AI.tldr: This review surveys seven advanced optical microscopy modalities for pathological imaging, their physical principles and representative applications, and discusses AI-assisted reconstruction/analysis and multimodal integration toward clinical translation.
AI.motivation: Histopathology is the gold standard for pathology imaging, but bright-field imaging is largely morphological. Advanced optical microscopy can exploit diverse light-matter interactions to provide quantitative or semi-quantitative information on tissue structure, mechanics, and chemical or molecular composition.
AI.method: The authors review optical diffraction tomography, polarisation microscopy, second-harmonic generation microscopy, third-harmonic generation microscopy, Brillouin microscopy, Raman microscopy, and fluorescence microscopy, summarising their physical principles, key quantitative parameters, and representative pathological applications; they also discuss AI for reconstruction, analysis, and interpretation and emerging multimodal integration.
AI.result: The review shows that diverse optical contrasts can complement routine histopathology by capturing signals such as refractive index, polarisation, harmonic generation, Brillouin shift, and molecular vibrations. No specific numerical or clinical performance results are provided because this is a review.
AI.conclusion: Advanced optical microscopy modalities can complement routine histopathology, but challenges and opportunities remain that will shape their clinical translation, with AI and multimodal integration as emerging trends.

title: Self-injection-locked dark-soliton Kerr optical frequency combs with high even-order normal dispersion
comment: 4 pages, 4 figures, to be published in Optics Letters
summary: We numerically investigate dissipative dark-soliton (DDS) microcombs under the action of pure high even-order normal (HEON) dispersion in a microresonator with the self-injection locking (SIL). Pure 4th, 6th, 10th, and 14th-order normal dispersion can support DDSs formed by interlocked switching waves, directly excited through a SIL-based turnkey scheme without detuning sweeps. Compared to the pure 4th-order case, the switching-wave tail oscillation period increases and its decay rate decreases with the increase of the dispersion order. Although the overall comb bandwidth narrows, the number of non-pump comb lines above a common absolute power threshold increases. Furthermore, the feedback phase controls the DDS duty cycle and intracavity comb-line power distribution, while the increase of the pump power improves the estimated pump-to-comb output conversion efficiency.

AI.tldr: This numerical study shows that pure high even-order normal dispersion in a self-injection-locked microresonator supports turnkey dissipative dark-soliton Kerr microcombs excited without detuning sweeps, with dispersion order, feedback phase, and pump power controlling switching-wave tails, comb-line distribution, and conversion efficiency.

They examine direct turnkey excitation without detuning sweeps, switching-wave tail oscillation and decay, comb bandwidth and non-pump comb-line counts above a common absolute power threshold, feedback-phase control of duty cycle and intracavity comb-line power distribution, and pump-power effects on estimated pump-to-comb output conversion efficiency.

Relative to the pure 4th-order case, increasing dispersion order increases the switching-wave tail oscillation period and decreases its decay rate. Although overall comb bandwidth narrows, the number of non-pump comb lines above a common absolute power threshold increases. Feedback phase controls the dark-soliton duty cycle and intracavity comb-line power distribution, while increasing pump power improves the estimated pump-to-comb output conversion efficiency.

title: Differential chiral sensing at exceptional points in intrinsically chiral metastructures
summary: Discriminating opposite enantiomers through their weak chiroptical responses remains a fundamental challenge in optical sensing. Exceptional points (EPs), non-Hermitian singularities at which eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, offer a route to enhanced spectral responses through their characteristic square-root eigenvalue splitting. However, their potential for chiral discrimination remains largely unexplored. We demonstrate exceptional points in an intrinsically chiral hybrid metamaterial and reveal strongly asymmetric responses to enantiomeric perturbations. The interplay between intrinsic chirality and non-Hermitian degeneracy is realized through the coupling of a chiral plasmonic nanoantenna array to a photonic crystal slab. We observe characteristic complex-square-root scaling, with both resonance frequencies and loss-rates exhibiting pronounced handedness dependence. Remarkably, opposite enantiomers produce complex mode splittings that differ by more than an order of magnitude. Our findings establish intrinsic chirality as a new degree of freedom in non-Hermitian physics and reveal a fundamental route toward topological singularities enhanced discrimination of chiral matter.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates exceptional points in an intrinsically chiral hybrid metamaterial formed by a chiral plasmonic nanoantenna array coupled to a photonic crystal slab, and shows strongly asymmetric, handedness-dependent complex mode splitting for opposite enantiomers.
AI.motivation: Weak chiroptical responses make discrimination of opposite enantiomers a fundamental challenge in optical sensing. Exceptional points offer enhanced spectral responses via square-root eigenvalue splitting, but their potential for chiral discrimination remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors realize exceptional points in an intrinsically chiral hybrid metamaterial by coupling a chiral plasmonic nanoantenna array to a photonic crystal slab. They analyze the non-Hermitian response, including resonance frequencies and loss rates, and compare complex mode splittings produced by opposite enantiomeric perturbations. The abstract does not provide material, fabrication, or operating-wavelength details.
AI.result: The system exhibits characteristic complex-square-root scaling, with pronounced handedness dependence in both resonance frequencies and loss rates. Opposite enantiomers produce complex mode splittings differing by more than an order of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic chirality is established as a new degree of freedom in non-Hermitian physics and as a fundamental route toward topological-singularity-enhanced discrimination of chiral matter.

title: Laser-Direct-Written polymer WGM microring laser integrated on a fiber tip for refractive index sensing
summary: Whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) microlasers are promising for refractometric sensing, but their practical implementation can be limited by the need for stable resonator-coupler alignment. Here, we demonstrate a Rhodamine B-doped polymer WGM microring laser directly fabricated on an optical-fiber tip, eliminating the external resonator-fiber coupling interface at the sensing head. Micro-droplet coating and UV laser direct writing are combined for fabrication, while finite-difference time-domain simulations guide the microring laser design. title: Deep-UV All-dielectric qBIC Metasurface for Refractive Index Sensing
summary: All-dielectric metasurfaces supporting quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) have emerged as powerful platforms for biosensing, yet their operation remains largely concentrated in the visible and near-infrared regimes. title: Modulation Induced Memory Resonances in Dynamically Driven Optical Cavities
summary: Temporal modulation of optical cavities provides a powerful mechanism for controlling photonic states beyond the static cavity paradigm. Here, we investigate the dynamics of periodically driven optical cavities using a time-dependent cavity-field model with modulated resonance frequencies. The interplay between periodic modulation and cavity dissipation gives rise to pronounced hysteretic behavior, revealing memory effects associated with the finite photon lifetime of the cavity. By quantifying the hysteresis area as a function of modulation frequency, we identify distinct memory resonances characterized by enhanced field-history dependence at specific driving frequencies. Furthermore, we examine the time-resolved local density of optical states (LDOS) and show that temporal modulation enables dynamic spectral redistribution of photonic states, with the degree of confinement governed by the cavity loss rate. Our results establish a simple framework for understanding and engineering memory effects in dynamically driven optical resonators and provide new opportunities for tunable photonic environments, dynamic LDOS control, and reconfigurable light-matter interactions.

title: Tailoring resonator geometry for astigmatism compensation with structured light in birefringent optical cavities
summary: In this work, we experimentally investigate the astigmatism induced by a birefringent crystal inside an optical cavity and demonstrate a geometric compensation strategy for structured modes carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM). We show that the astigmatism observed in the semimonolithic configuration can be fully compensated by introducing a third mirror to fold the cavity, thereby exploiting the geometric astigmatism arising from oblique incidence on the curved mirror. By performing a study of the resonator geometry, both theoretical and experimental results confirm that this approach enables the preservation of OAM between the pump beam and the converted signal and idler modes, providing an effective design strategy for birefringent optical cavities.

title: Discrete time crystals and heteroclinic switching in actively mode-locked semiconductor lasers

title: Universal photonic synthetic temporal-mode converter for heterogeneous quantum interconnects
summary: We propose a synthetic temporal-mode converter (STC) that combines programmable waveform matching with denser time multiplexing for heterogeneous quantum interconnects. Simulations yield mode overlaps above 99.9\% for exponential and Gaussian inputs. For $N=256$ and $0.5\,\mathrm{dB}$ loss per stage, STC gives a 45.6-fold higher photon-pair coincidence rate than temporal gating at equal mode overlap for two exponential inputs. title: Shaping Frequency-Bin Biphoton Correlations via Programmable Optical Frequency Combs
summary: Programmable shaping of photon-pair spectral correlations is important for frequency-bin quantum information processing. However, achieving this control remains challenging in nonlinear optical systems without reliable forward models. Here, we demonstrate model-free, hardware-in-the-loop shaping of the measured joint spectral intensity of a cascaded photon-pair source driven by a programmable optical frequency comb. A blockwise simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation controller optimizes up to 22 pump, signal, and idler parameters. Each iteration requires only two accepted hardware evaluations, independent of the parameter count. The controller converges to diverse target patterns on 3$\times$3, 4$\times$4, and 5$\times$5 frequency-bin grids. The optimized distributions achieve Pearson correlations between 0.66 and 0.98 and classical overlap fidelities between 0.32 and 0.62. Cross-target similarity analysis confirms that the optimized patterns remain target-specific. Source characterization yields a maximum coincidence-to-accidental ratio of approximately 585. Accuracy is limited by pump-phase transfer, parasitic nonlinear background, waveshaper constraints, amplitude-only filtering, and measurement noise. Joint spectral intensity contains no spectral-phase information. Therefore, the results demonstrate control of measured frequency-bin populations and correlations, not complete reconstruction of the two-photon state. Phase-sensitive characterization is required to verify inter-bin coherence and quantify the entanglement dimensionality of the output state. title: Cavity-enhanced second harmonic generation from Rydberg excitons in Cu$_2$O
summary: Rydberg excitons in Cu$_2$O provide a solid-state setting for creating giant optical nonlinearities. Here, we use second-harmonic generation (SHG) to study Rydberg excitons in a doubly resonant optical microcavity designed to enhance both the pump and second-harmonic fields. We observe even-parity exciton states in an optical cavity and extend cavity-based measurements of Rydberg excitons up to $n=10$. The SHG intensity depends strongly on pump cavity detuning, showing the dominant role of the microcavity is the enhancement of the intra-cavity pump field. Analysis reveals an additional enhancement from the resonant second-harmonic cavity giving an overall SHG enhancement factor of $21 \pm 2$ inside the microcavity. title: Inversion symmetry breaking by interlayer hybridization in a tetralayer van der Waals heterostructure
summary: Inversion symmetry breaking unlocks a broad range of physical phenomena fundamental for modern technologies, motivating efforts to engineer noncentrosymmetric materials. In this context, monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides, which naturally lack inversion symmetry, have emerged as a versatile platform for valley physics, strong excitonic effects, and nonlinear optics. However, in their hexagonal stacking phase, inversion symmetry is restored in even-layer stacks and bulk form, suppressing these effects and limiting applications. In this work, inversion symmetry breaking is demonstrated in a vertically stacked tetralayer heterostructure assembled from two intrinsically centrosymmetric bilayer flakes, as evidenced by second harmonic generation measurements with an intensity comparable to that of their constituent monolayer. Spectroscopic measurements and theoretical estimations indicate that effective symmetry breaking in the tetralayer heterostructure is driven by interlayer hybridization, giving rise to pronounced electronic and phononic signatures. This symmetry breaking further induces polar anisotropy, with an intensity ratio reaching 2.36. We propose that asymmetric contributions from excitons to the second harmonic optical dipole may influence this behavior. These findings establish interlayer coupling as a critical mechanism for introducing inversion symmetry breaking and tuning the optical response of van der Waals heterostructures, providing a powerful strategy for photonics and optoelectronics in two-dimensional materials.

title: Absolute Calibration of a Broadband Transmission Grating Spectrometer from 5 to 400 nm with Uncertainty Estimates
summary: We present the absolute calibration of a transmission grating spectrometer (TGS) with uncertainty estimates in the 5--400 nm range using synchrotron radiation at the BEAR beamline at Elettra light source in Trieste, Italy. Next, the quantum efficiency of the spectrometer's CCD camera was calibrated over the 5--400 nm range. Lastly, three gratings with line densities of 10000, 3000, and 1000 lines/mm were calibrated for spectroscopy in the ranges extending from soft X-ray to extreme-, vacuum- and deep-ultraviolet (DUV) wavelengths, respectively. title: Disentangling Spin and Orbital Contributions in the Search for Altermagnetic Terahertz Conversion in RuO2
summary: Rutile RuO2 has emerged as a prominent candidate altermagnet, yet the microscopic origin of its reported charge-angular-momentum conversion remains unsettled. Here, we report the first experimental disentanglement of the spin- and orbital-to-charge conversion channels in RuO2 heterostructures using terahertz emission spectroscopy. We identify Fe as a predominantly spin-current injector, whereas Ni and permalloy predominantly inject orbital currents, revealing a substantial orbital contribution to ultrafast terahertz emission. Under controlled spin-current injection, we find no evidence for inverse altermagnetic spin-splitting effect. Instead, the observed anisotropy is consistent with an anisotropic inverse spin Hall response that is strongly conditioned by the near-interface environment. Under orbital-current injection, the anisotropy is markedly weaker, indicating that orbital-to-charge conversion is largely isotropic in RuO2. Our results establish orbital transport and interface-conditioned spin Hall conversion as key to terahertz emission from RuO2, underscoring the need to disentangle spin, orbital, and interfacial contributions before assigning anisotropy to altermagnetism.

title: Talanov dynamics and chirp-controlled rogue-wave formation for the vector nonlinear Schrödinger equation
summary: We study the focusing vector nonlinear Schrödinger equation, or Manakov system, for a pair of coupled initial conditions with compactly supported, concave parabolic density profiles and phases depending quadratically on the spatial coordinate. We focus on the natural class of self-similar solutions generated by such profiles, whose dispersionless evolution we refer to as Talanov dynamics. We extend the criterion for blow-up in finite time, first established for a single field, to the Manakov case. For arbitrary initial chirps in the two fields, we provide closed-form expressions for their evolution, and an explicit expression for the time of the gradient catastrophe, if it occurs, and we classify the effect of the coupling on the catastrophe. Depending on the initial chirps, the two fields may catastrophise, or relax, as each would if decoupled. However, coupling can also force the catastrophe in fields that would otherwise relax if decoupled. For identical initial supports, and in the presence of dispersion, we numerically show that the same dispersionless criterion determines, in the semiclassical regime, whether the fully dispersive solution relaxes or develops a rogue wave in each field, whose onset time is accurately predicted by the corresponding dispersionless catastrophe time, in direct analogy with the scalar case. As chirp and amplitude are relatively easy to control experimentally, we expect these results to be relevant to experiments in nonlinear optics and Bose-Einstein condensates, extending to coupled systems observations made for the scalar equation.
